01

The headline sells the promise, not the product name.

Leading with a product promise in the headline — rather than the product name — gives visitors immediate context before they read a single line of body copy. This is one of the clearest opportunities to add upfront value in our next builds.

✓ Breanden — promise-led headline
"The Last Skillet You'll Ever Buy™"
"The Last Air Purifier You'll Ever Buy"
"Make every day a great hair day."
→ Our pages — opportunity to lead with a promise
"The Keeper Apron" — product name
"Name Big 2" — product name
"Noctis" — product name
What Breanden does

H1 = outcome for the buyer. Product name appears as a small eyebrow label — never the main headline.

Where we can improve

H1 = product name. The value prop lives in body copy below — moving it up into the headline is a quick, high-impact upgrade.

The fix

Move product name to an eyebrow. Rewrite H1 as a one-sentence promise. 5 min per page — highest leverage change on this list.

02

More breathing room between sections makes the scroll feel like an experience, not a document.

When each section has one idea and generous vertical padding, the scroll develops rhythm — each idea has room to land before the next one starts. Increasing section spacing is one of the most impactful structural changes we can make.

✓ Breanden — wide open sections
✓ Air Purifier
80–120px padding per section. One headline, 2–3 lines of copy, one image. The scroll has natural rhythm — each section feels like a pause before the next idea.
Work Pants — next steps
Opportunity: increase section padding. Feature icons, copy blocks, and lifestyle images are close together — spreading these out with ~80–100px of breathing room between sections would immediately improve the reading rhythm.
✓ Iron Skillet
Sections feel like chapters. Negative space signals each thought is complete before the next arrives. The visitor fully processes one idea before the next appears.
Noctis — next steps
Opportunity: give each section more room. The mid-page has multiple content blocks in close succession. Spreading these out would let each idea land before the next one arrives.
The symptom

When sections have generous spacing, scrolling feels like reading chapters. Adding breathing room to our pages moves them in that direction.

The cause

More sections are packed into the same scroll depth. Fewer sections, more space each — that's the edit needed.

The fix

Set min 100px padding top/bottom per section. Merge adjacent sections that cover the same idea. Pure CSS — no content changes needed.

03

Letting feature sections stretch edge to edge is the next level.

Feature sections that span the full viewport — image column bleeding to the screen edge, text column filling the other half — give pages a much stronger visual presence. Our pages have the right content structure; removing the max-width container is the single change that unlocks this.

✓ Iron Skillet
Full-viewport alternating rows. Image bleeds to the left screen edge. Text runs to the right edge. No outer container. The screen is fully owned.
Apron — next steps
Opportunity: remove the max-width container. Image and text both sit inside a centered wrapper — letting the image column bleed to the screen edge would immediately create a more immersive, full-width feel.
✓ Air Purifier
Feature rows bleed edge to edge. The filter section — carbon pellet photography left, text right — fills 100vw. Neither column has outer margins.
Work Pants — next steps
Opportunity: full-viewport feature rows. Content stays within the centered wrapper — on a wide screen there's unused space on both sides. Going edge-to-edge here would make a noticeable difference.
✓ Showerhead
Product photography owns the viewport. In-use shots run to the screen edge. Text flanks at full width. The product feels physically large on the page.
Noctis — next steps
Opportunity: let photography own more space. Lifestyle photos sit within the layout container — pushing one or two of these to the full viewport width would let the product photography breathe and make a stronger impression.
The pattern to copy

Alternating full-width rows: image 55vw · text 45vw, then flipped. No max-width on the row. Text column has internal padding; image column bleeds fully.

Why it works

Full-width sections force the eye to travel the whole screen — buying dwell time. The visitor spends more time on each section before the CTA arrives.

The fix

Remove max-width from feature section wrappers. CSS change only — no content changes needed.

04

Adding a second product selector at the bottom closes a high-intent gap.

A visitor who scrolls all the way to the bottom of a PDP is the most convinced person on the page — they read everything. Surfacing the product selector again at the bottom means they can act on that conviction immediately, without having to scroll back up to find the buy button.

✓ Breanden — product form repeated at bottom
Skillet — full product form at bottom
Air Purifier — variants + CTA at page end
Showerhead — buy section closes the page
→ Our pages — opportunity to add a closing product form
Apron — opportunity: add closing product form
Work Pants — opportunity: add closing product form
Noctis — opportunity: add closing product form
Why this spot matters most

Bottom-of-page visitors read everything. They are the most convinced people on the page. Removing friction here is the highest-leverage CTA placement possible.

Breanden's exact pattern

Full product form: variant selectors → quantity → price → "Add to Cart." Not just a button — the full selector so the action is completed inline without scrolling.

The fix

Copy the hero product form component. Paste as second-to-last section on every PDP, just before the final closing line. One component reuse per page.

05

Shifting toward more pictures than words speeds up comprehension.

For a physical product, a photograph communicates texture, quality, and use case faster than any sentence. Our pages have solid copy — the opportunity is to let imagery carry more of the load on the next build, so visitors can feel the product before they even finish reading.

✓ Iron Skillet
Image-dominant sections. Photography fills the majority of every section. Text is 2–4 lines confirming what the image already shows — you understand the product before finishing the copy.
→ Work Pants
Opportunity: let images lead. Feature descriptions and specs carry the load right now — giving images more section area and trimming copy to 3–5 lines per section would shift this toward a see-first experience.
✓ Air Purifier
Full-bleed detail photography. A section dedicated to the carbon filter macro shot. No paragraph needed — the image communicates material quality and specificity in one glance.
→ Apron
Opportunity: show the craftsmanship, don't just describe it. Increasing image size and reducing surrounding copy would let the material quality speak for itself — the photography is there, it just needs more room.
✓ Showerhead
In-use lifestyle photography leads. Product shown in real context at large scale. Text is sparse — a headline and 2–3 lines. The image sells the experience; the copy confirms it.
→ Noctis
Opportunity: give the photography more room. The blanket's texture and weight are best communicated visually — expanding those images and trimming the surrounding copy would make the product feel more tangible.
✓ Breanden — estimated page composition
65% image area 35% text / copy
→ Our pages — estimated page composition
35% image area 65% text / copy
The principle

When an image can say it, let it. The goal is for visitors to feel the product before they finish reading — not to make them read their way to understanding it.

The blocker

Getting more product photography — macro, detail, in-use shots — is the enabler here. Understanding Breanden's image generation workflow would help unlock this for our next builds.

What to do now

For every text + thumbnail section: expand image to 60% of section area, reduce copy to 3–5 lines. Information stays — the feel changes completely.

5 observations.
4 are structural.
1 needs better assets.

Four of the five are structural or copy decisions we can action on the next PDP build right away. The fifth is about leveling up the image assets — something we can explore and improve on as we go.
